newsitem.title: PERU: Poverty and inequality foment Peru rebel groups.
newsitem.headline: Poverty and inequality foment Peru rebel groups.

text.p: The now-infamous high-society party at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima was a stark contrast to the grinding poverty suffered by millions of Peruvians that has fuelled Peru's guerrilla movements.

Inside the elegant compound in the upscale San Isidro district last Tuesday, Peru's elite -- generals, ministers, businessmen, diplomats, and relatives of President Alberto Fujimori -- sipped cocktails and enjoyed a sumptuous buffet.

They were blissfully unaware of what was awaiting them as about 20 Marxist rebels prepared to blow a hole in the wall and take them hostage in one of the most spectacular guerrilla assaults of Latin America's troubled history. The rebels, members of the Cuban-inspired Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) who are based in the jungle far from Lima, claim to be acting on behalf of Peru's impoverished masses.

"The MRTA was born in the country to struggle for the problems that marginalize the large majority of Peruvians, especially in the period of the government of President Alberto Fujimori that also worsened and increased poverty dramatically in Peru," it said a statement issued on Sunday night when 225 hostages were released.

The rebels, who still hold 140 captives including top Peruvian government leaders, are bargaining for demands that include a call to restructure the economy to help the poor. While the government condemns them as terrorists, and few in Peru agree with the MRTA's violent tactics, most analysts acknowledge that the Andean country's social problems are a root cause of 16 years of guerrilla conflict and the current hostage crisis.
"It is an important element among the various factors that produce a revolutionary movement," Guillermo Rochabru, a sociologist at Lima's Catholic University, said.

"If anything, the social situation in Peru is getting worse," added John Crabtree, Latin American editor at Oxford Analitica, a British-based news analysis consultancy. Poverty has been barely touched in Fujimori's six-year tenure and the gap between rich and poor has grown, he said.

"This combination of marginalization with inadequate political representation within the domestic political system means that (guerrilla movements) are always bound to be a problem," he said. "In Peru, there are not the channels through which social tensions can be expressed."

Even according to government figures, which human rights and social groups dispute, poverty afflicts 47 percent of this nation of 24 million inhabitants. About 19 percent live in extreme poverty, the government says.

In Lima, at least half of the 6 million inhabitants live in shantytowns ringing the capital where water is scarce and garbage dumps are meticulously raked over for scraps of food. Other signs of poverty -- street children, beggars, malnutrition -- are depresssingly familiar on Lima's streets.

But the biggest contrast is in highland or jungle provinces, where in many areas illiterate Peruvian peasants live at subsistence level in isolated communities with none of the amenities of modern life.

"It is like going back to a previous century when you travel into the provinces," a Western diplomat in Lima said. "I don't know how they can live like that, totally forgotten -- a very, very hard life. It's inevitable that some won't tolerate it, and there'll be a backlash against those who have left them behind."

While Fujimori's radical free-market economic reforms have brought Peru back into the international financial community's fold, and pulled the economy from chaos, they have not yet made a significant impact on poverty levels. Opinion polls show low wage levels and unemployment as among Peruvians' major concerns.

"Fujimori has to realise that the people are running out of patience. We have suffered a lot and not yet gained anything here," taxi driver Lorenzo Mesones said, tapping his pocket. "This attack has to be seen in the context of intolerable suffering by the people. It was an explosion waiting to happen. If not from them, then others would have done it."
The MRTA and the better known Maoist Shining Path were all but defeated by Fujimori after the capture of their leaders in 1992, but both have made a resurgence this year.

"In the past, the terrorists massacred the little people and no one took any notice. Now they've got all the rich people in there, but the rest of us aren't really affected in a practical way," said Manuel Serrano, who makes a long daily trek to San Isidro from the Lima shantytown of Villa Salvador to sell fruit.
"I don't support them at all but I can't exactly blame them 100 percent because they say they are doing it for people like me who have no voice or place in this society."
